{{Short description|Type of morphism in algebraic geometry}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a [[morphism]] ''f'' : ''X'' &rarr; ''Y'' of [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] is  '''quasi-finite''' if it is of [[Morphism of finite type|finite type]] and satisfies any of the following equivalent conditions:<ref>EGA II, Définition 6.2.3</ref>

* Every point ''x'' of ''X'' is isolated in its fiber ''f''<sup>&minus;1</sup>(''f''(''x'')).  In other words, every [[Fiber (algebraic geometry)|fiber]] is a discrete (hence finite) set.
* For every point ''x'' of ''X'', the scheme {{nowrap|''f''<sup>&minus;1</sup>(''f''(''x'')) {{=}} ''X'' &times;<sub>Y</sub>Spec &kappa;(''f''(''x''))}} is a [[finite morphism|finite]] &kappa;(''f''(''x''))-scheme.  (Here &kappa;(''p'') is the [[residue field]] at a point ''p''.)
* For every point ''x'' of ''X'', <math>\mathcal{O}_{X,x}\otimes \kappa(f(x))</math> is finitely generated over <math>\kappa(f(x))</math>.

Quasi-finite morphisms were originally defined by [[Alexander Grothendieck]] in [[Séminaire de géométrie algébrique|SGA]] 1 and did not include the finite type hypothesis.  This hypothesis was added to the definition in [[Éléments de géométrie algébrique|EGA]] II 6.2 because it makes it possible to give an algebraic characterization of quasi-finiteness in terms of [[Stalk (sheaf)|stalks]].

For a general morphism {{nowrap|''f'' : ''X'' &rarr; ''Y''}} and a point ''x'' in ''X'', ''f'' is said to be '''quasi-finite''' at ''x'' if there exist open affine neighborhoods ''U'' of ''x'' and ''V'' of ''f''(''x'') such that ''f''(''U'') is contained in ''V'' and such that the restriction {{nowrap|''f'' : ''U'' &rarr; ''V''}} is quasi-finite.  ''f'' is '''locally quasi-finite''' if it is quasi-finite at every point in ''X''.<ref>EGA III, Err<sub>III</sub>, 20.</ref>  A [[Quasi-compact morphism|quasi-compact]] locally quasi-finite morphism is quasi-finite.

== Properties ==
For a morphism ''f'', the following properties are true.<ref name=autogenerated1>EGA II, Proposition 6.2.4.</ref>
* If ''f'' is quasi-finite, then the induced map ''f''<sub>red</sub> between [[reduced scheme]]s is quasi-finite.
* If ''f'' is a [[closed immersion]], then ''f'' is quasi-finite.
* If ''X'' is [[noetherian scheme|noetherian]] and ''f'' is an immersion, then ''f'' is quasi-finite.
* If {{nowrap|g : ''Y'' &rarr; ''Z''}}, and if {{nowrap|''g'' ∘ ''f''}} is quasi-finite, then ''f'' is quasi-finite if any of the following are true:
*#''g'' is [[separated morphism|separated]],
*#''X'' is noetherian,
*#{{nowrap|''X'' &times;<sub>''Z''</sub> ''Y''}} is locally noetherian.

Quasi-finiteness is preserved by base change.  The composite and fiber product of quasi-finite morphisms is quasi-finite.<ref name=autogenerated1 />

If ''f'' is [[Glossary of scheme theory#Unramified and étale morphisms|unramified]] at a point ''x'', then ''f'' is quasi-finite at ''x''.  Conversely, if ''f'' is quasi-finite at ''x'', and if also <math>\mathcal{O}_{f^{-1}(f(x)),x}</math>, the [[local ring]] of ''x'' in the fiber ''f''<sup>&minus;1</sup>(''f''(''x'')), is a field and a [[finite extension|finite]] [[separable extension]] of &kappa;(''f''(''x'')), then ''f'' is unramified at ''x''.<ref>EGA IV<sub>4</sub>, Théorème 17.4.1.</ref>

[[Finite morphism]]s are quasi-finite.<ref>EGA II, Corollaire 6.1.7.</ref>  A quasi-finite [[proper morphism]] locally of finite presentation is finite.<ref>EGA IV<sub>3</sub>, Théorème 8.11.1.</ref> Indeed, a morphism is finite [[if and only if]] it is proper and locally quasi-finite.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02LS |website=[[The Stacks Project]] |access-date=31 January 2022 |title=Lemma 02LS}}</ref> Since proper morphisms are of finite type and finite type morphisms are quasi-compact<ref>{{cite web |url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01T1 |website=The Stacks Project |access-date=15 August 2023 |title=Definition 29.15.1.}}</ref> one may omit the qualification ''locally'', i.e., a morphism is finite if and only if it is proper and quasi-finite.

A generalized form of '''[[Zariski Main Theorem]]''' is the following:<ref>EGA IV<sub>3</sub>, Théorème 8.12.6.</ref> Suppose ''Y'' is [[compact space#Introduction and definition|quasi-compact]] and [[quasi-separated]]. Let ''f'' be quasi-finite, separated and of finite presentation. Then ''f'' factors as <math> X \hookrightarrow X' \to Y</math> where the first morphism is an open immersion and the second is finite. (''X'' is open in a finite scheme over ''Y''.)
